Waiting for a dip before investing each paycheque: test the rule against regular purchases

Hold new monthly savings in cash until the market falls by a set amount, or invest each deposit as it arrives. Compare the cash queue, the purchase prices and the ending value across three authored paths.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Both rules receive the same $500 at each of 36 month-ends. The regular rule buys at that close. The waiting rule holds new cash and buys all of it at the first close at least 10% below the running peak, or once the oldest waiting deposit has waited 12 months. The authored paths are teaching examples, not historical returns, forecasts or likelihoods. No trading costs, tax, fund fees, distributions or settlement delay are modeled; waiting cash earns the entered effective annual rate converted to a monthly rate.

The central idea

A buy-the-dip rule for new pay turns every paycheque into a timing decision. Cash can earn interest while it waits, but the rule can miss a rise, buy after a late dip at a higher price than earlier months, or never fire at all. Write the waiting limit before the first deposit.

01

The question is about new money, not an existing lump sum

Many regular savers invest each deposit soon after their pay arrives. A common alternative is to hold new savings in cash and invest only after prices fall: “I will buy when the market is 10% below its high.” This guide tests that rule for money that arrives monthly from earnings.

That is a different decision from staging a lump sum already on hand. With a lump sum, phased purchases leave part of an existing balance in cash by design; the lump-sum comparison covers that case. FINRA notes that the cash-drag concern applies mainly when a pool of cash is waiting, and that contributions invested as they are earned do not sit idle. A dip rule recreates a cash pool out of new pay.

The model gives both rules the same deposit at each of 36 month-ends. The regular rule buys at that month’s close. The waiting rule holds the deposit in cash, earns the entered interest rate, and buys everything waiting at the first close that is at least the trigger percentage below the highest close observed so far, or once the oldest waiting deposit reaches the entered waiting limit.

02

Waiting cash earns a rate, and prices keep moving too

The first chart places two dated public figures side by side. Statistics Canada reported that all-items CPI rose 3.1% year over year in September 2026. The Bank of Canada’s target for the overnight rate was 2.25% on 22 October 2026. A deposit account, GIC or money market fund can pay a different rate, and neither figure says what inflation or interest will be while your cash waits.

The scenario uses a separate cash rate, set by default to 2.25% as an illustration. Interest earned outside a registered account is generally taxable; tax is not deducted in the model. Inside a TFSA, CRA says income earned is generally tax-free, but a deposit still uses contribution room whether the money stays in cash or buys a fund. The account sets the tax rules; the investment inside it still carries its own risk, fees and liquidity terms.

03

A trigger based on the running peak can fire late, or not at all

The index chart shows the authored index and the trigger line, which follows the running peak. Because the peak keeps rising in a long advance, a dip can begin well above prices that regular purchases already paid. In the default early dip, then recovery path, the 10% trigger first fires at month five. Waiting cash is then invested through month ten while the index stays below the line. After the recovery, new deposits wait again until the 12-month limit forces purchases at months 23 and 36.

Under these defaults, the regular rule ends at about CAD 21,127 and the waiting rule at about CAD 20,760, including interest on waiting cash. The waiting rule’s average cost per unit is about 103.93 index points, versus 101.25 for investing every month. It caught a dip but paid more on average because later deposits waited through the rise.

The path comparison shows why one example settles nothing. On the steady rise path the 10% trigger never fires, so purchases happen only when the waiting limit forces them; the regular rule ends ahead, CAD 19,214 versus CAD 19,003. On the long rise, late dip path the waiting rule ends ahead, CAD 18,826 versus CAD 18,603. Neither result is a probability or a backtest.

04

The waiting limit is the rule’s most important setting

Set the waiting limit to zero and the waiting rule becomes regular investing: each deposit is bought at the close on which it arrives. Raise the limit and the rule can hold more money in cash for longer. If the trigger never arrives, the cash queue can keep growing, and so can the gap if prices rise.

FINRA’s market-timing guidance warns that short-term price moves are difficult to predict and that some of the strongest market days can occur during volatile periods. A rule written in advance avoids changing the threshold after seeing prices, but it does not make the decision free. Before using a dip trigger, decide:

  • the exact trigger and the price series it uses;
  • the longest time any deposit may wait;
  • where waiting cash is held, what it earns and how it is taxed;
  • whether purchases have commissions, spreads or fund minimums;
  • whether the investment’s risk still suits the goal if the dip deepens after you buy.

05

If the worry is a crash, adjust the mix instead of the calendar

Concern about a large decline is reasonable, especially near a spending date. Holding every new deposit until a dip mixes two decisions: how much risk the portfolio should carry and when to buy it. Often the clearer adjustment is the allocation itself, for example a balanced fund with a bond portion, a larger cash reserve for near-term spending, or a smaller monthly amount that the budget can sustain through an income interruption.

Regular investing does not avoid losses or guarantee a lower cost per unit. It does keep each deposit’s purchase date tied to when money is earned rather than to a forecast. Read the selected fund’s Fund Facts for its risk rating, fees and holdings, and review the account’s contribution and withdrawal rules separately. The companion guides on exiting and re-entering the market and keeping a cash floor beside regular purchases test related rules.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. The September 2026 CPI change and the 22 October 2026 Bank of Canada target for the overnight rate are dated official observations. All index paths, triggers, waiting limits, cash rates and balances are hypothetical editable calculations, not historical returns or forecasts.
